Although participation makes up a large part of the final grade, in practice, only the same two or three students dominate class discussions. The instructor does not actively encourage wider participation, and classes often turn into prolonged dialogues with the same individuals, which discourages others from attending. In some sessions, nearly the entire 50-minute class was spent in continuous dialogue with a single student.
Additionally, grading feels excessively strict. Even when students seek feedback and revise their work accordingly, evaluations seem focused on point deductions rather than improvement. While the instructor is clearly knowledgeable and enthusiastic about philosophy, the course would benefit from more inclusive discussion management and clearer, more supportive grading practices.

instructor:
Just don’t take this course from him. He is enthusiastic about teaching, but that doesn’t matter when the grading is excessively harsh and rigid.

In our section, the highest first essay grade was 85, which would be considered a low-to-mid grade in other professors’ sections such as Tufan’s or Berkowski’s. This creates a clear inconsistency: students with similar academic levels in other sections are receiving 95+, while our section’s top grade is 85.

The participation grading was also inconsistent. He initially stated that simply attending lectures would not be enough and that students must actively participate to receive credit; otherwise, they would receive 0, which would be reasonable if applied consistently. However, he later gave a 14 to a student who never spoke in class but had perfect attendance, while other students who actively participated received lower scores simply because they did not have 100% attendance, directly contradicting his own stated criteria.

He also openly stated that only one student would receive a 15 for participation, one a 14, and the rest lower, calling this his “policy.”

So, because of his policy, even the people who has perfect grades from the English section of the course, no one will be able to get an A, because of his grading.
